title: Numbers, prices, and shopping
title_target: いくらですか — Ikura desu ka
goal: Count from zero up to the tens of thousands, ask prices, ask for things politely, and get through a whole shop transaction from start to finish.
bekal: ask the price with いくらですか
ask for things with ～をください
survive a checkout conversation from greeting to change

dialogs.title: 会話 1 — At the convenience store
dialogs.intro: Ani buys a few things. Notice that the cashier uses far more respectful language than the customer — that's normal, and you don't need to match it.

lines.speaker: てんいん:
lines.text: [いらっしゃいませ|Irasshaimase]。

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [すみません|Sumimasen]。[この|kono] [ノートは|nōto wa] [いくらですか|ikura desu ka]。
lines.id: Excuse me. How much is this notebook?
lines.literal: excuse-me. this — notebook — as-for — how-much — is — [question]

lines.speaker: てんいん:
lines.text: [それは|Sore wa] 250[えんです|en desu]。

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [じゃあ|Jā]、[それを|sore o] [みっつ|mittsu] [ください|kudasai]。

lines.speaker: てんいん:
lines.text: [はい|Hai]、[みっつですね|mittsu desu ne]。[ほかには|Hoka ni wa]？
lines.literal: yes, three-things — is — right. other — in — as-for?

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [この|Kono] [ペンも|pen mo] [ください|kudasai]。[いくらですか|Ikura desu ka]。
lines.id: This pen too, please. How much is it?
lines.literal: this — pen — also — please-give. how-much — is — [question]

lines.speaker: てんいん:
lines.text: [ペンは|Pen wa] 120[えんです|en desu]。[ぜんぶで|Zenbu de] 870[えんです|en desu]。
lines.id: The pen is 120 yen. That's 870 yen altogether.
lines.literal: pen — as-for — 120 — yen — is. all — with — 870 — yen — is.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [カードで|Kādo de] [いいですか|ii desu ka]。

lines.speaker: てんいん:
lines.text: [はい|Hai]、[だいじょうぶです|daijōbu desu]。

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [おねがいします|Onegaishimasu]。

lines.speaker: てんいん:
lines.text: [ありがとうございました|Arigatō gozaimashita]。[またどうぞ|Mata dōzo]。
lines.id: Thank you very much. Please come again.

notes: **～をください = “please give me ～”.** The single most useful way to ask for anything in Japan: メニューをください, みずをください, これをください. Polite, clear, and never out of place in a shop or restaurant.

**The number comes after the noun, not before.** English: *three notebooks*. Japanese: ノートを**みっつ**ください — the noun first, the number after. This is the opposite of what you're used to, and it takes a few days to feel natural.
**ぜんぶで = “altogether”.** The particle で here marks a limit or total. You'll hear it at every checkout in Japan.
**～でいいですか = “is ～ OK?”.** カードでいいですか = can I pay by card? This short pattern covers many situations: えいごでいいですか (is English OK?).
**ありがとうございました with ました, not ます.** The past form is used when the business is **finished** — the cashier says it once the transaction is done. Before that, it's ありがとうございます.
**ほかには？** = “anything else?”. If you're done, answer いいえ、けっこうです (no, that's all) — けっこうです is a polite refusal worth memorizing.

grammars.title: Numbers 0 to 99,999
body: Japanese numbers are very regular. After ten, a number is read exactly the way it's built: 11 = 10 + 1 = [じゅういち|jūichi], 25 = 2 × 10 + 5 = [にじゅうご|nijūgo]. There are no special forms like English *eleven*, *twelve* or *-teen*.
after: ⚠️ **The marked ones change sound** because the consonants clash: [さんひゃく|sanhyaku] is too clumsy to say, so it becomes [さんびゃく|sanbyaku]. Don't learn this as a rule — just memorize these numbers: 300, 600, 800, 3,000, 8,000.

**10,000 is a unit of its own ([まん|man]), not “ten thousand”.** This is the hardest point for English speakers: a price of 25,000 yen is read **[にまんごせん|niman gosen]** (2 man 5 sen), not “twenty-five thousand”. The trick: split numbers from the right every **four** digits, not three.
**4, 7 and 9 have two readings.** Rule of thumb: use [よん|yon], [なな|nana], [きゅう|kyū]. The forms [し|shi], [しち|shichi], [く|ku] appear more in clock times and dates, and will be pointed out when needed.

grammars.title: Asking for things: ～[をください|o kudasai] and relatives
body: Three request patterns that cover almost everything you'll need as a beginner:

head: Pattern
Example
Used for
rows: [おかいけいを|Okaikei o] [おねがいします|onegaishimasu]。
A little more polite. Good for asking for **services**: please ring this up, please wrap it.
[トイレは|Toire wa] [ありますか|arimasu ka]。

after: ⚠️ **Don't use [ください|kudasai] to ask someone to do something** — that needs a different form ([て|te]-form + [ください|kudasai]), covered in Unit 10. [ください|kudasai] with [を|o] is for things only.

dialogs.title: 会話 2 — At the coffee shop
dialogs.intro: Budi orders a drink. Ordering in Japan has its own flow: order, size, for here or to go, pay.

lines.speaker: てんいん:
lines.text: [いらっしゃいませ|Irasshaimase]。[ごちゅうもんは|Gochūmon wa]？

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [アイスコーヒーを|Aisu kōhī o] [ひとつ|hitotsu] [ください|kudasai]。

lines.speaker: てんいん:
lines.text: [サイズは|Saizu wa]？ S、M、L [が|ga] [あります|arimasu]。
lines.id: What size? We have S, M, and L.
lines.literal: size — as-for? S, M, L — [subject] — exist.

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: M [を|o] [おねがいします|onegaishimasu]。

lines.speaker: てんいん:
lines.text: [こちらで|Kochira de] [おめしあがりですか|omeshiagari desu ka]。

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [いいえ|Iie]、[もちかえりで|mochikaeri de]。

lines.speaker: てんいん:
lines.text: [かしこまりました|Kashikomarimashita]。480[えんです|en desu]。

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: 1000[えんで|en de] [おねがいします|onegaishimasu]。
lines.id: Out of a thousand yen, please.

lines.speaker: てんいん:
lines.text: 520[えんの|en no] [おかえしです|okaeshi desu]。

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [どうも|Dōmo]。

lines.speaker: てんいん:
lines.text: [ありがとうございました|Arigatō gozaimashita]。

notes: **かしこまりました = “certainly”, in a very respectful form.** You'll hear it in restaurants, hotels, and on customer-service calls. You **don't need to use it** — it's staff speaking to customers. Just recognize it.
**おめしあがりですか is also one-way honorific language.** It means “will you be eating it (here)?”. You only need two answers: **はい** (here) or **もちかえりで** (to go).
**Paying with a larger bill.** 1000えんでおねがいします is the standard phrase when handing over money. で here means “with (a tool/means)”.

**ご before a word = the honorific version.** It does the same job as the お you saw in Unit 1, but is used with words of Chinese origin: ごちゅうもん, ごかぞく. Which words take お and which take ご isn't worth memorizing now — you'll pick them up one at a time.
**どうも on its own = a short thanks.** Fine between equals, a bit too casual for a boss. The full version is どうもありがとうございます.
**Sen and yen.** Yen is written 円 and pronounced **えん** (*en*), not “yen”. The English spelling “yen” is a historical leftover, not how it sounds.

grammars.title: Two ways of counting: [つ|tsu] and [こ|ko]
body: Japanese can't count without **counter words** — a bit like “three *sheets* of paper” or “two *loaves* of bread” in English, but compulsory. For a beginner, these two systems go a long way:

**～[つ|tsu] (native Japanese counting)** — for things in general, 1 to 10. The forms are irregular and must be memorized, but this is your lifesaver: if you don't know the right counter, ～[つ|tsu] is almost always understood.
**～[こ|ko] ([個|ko])** — for small, round objects; and from 11 upward, ～[つ|tsu] is no longer used.
after: ⚠️ **[ひとり|hitori] and [ふたり|futari] break the pattern** — 1 person and 2 people have their own forms; the rest use ～[にん|nin].
**Position in the sentence:** [ノートを|nōto o] **[みっつ|mittsu]** [ください|kudasai]。 The number stands on its own after the object, with no particle at all.

grammars.title: [で|de] — the “with” particle that does double duty
body: You'll meet the particle **[で|de]** again and again. In this unit it shows up in three jobs, all of which can be translated “with” or “by”:

head: Job
Example
Meaning
rows: [にほんごで|Nihongo de] [おねがいします|onegaishimasu]

after: [で|de] has one more big job — marking **the place where an action happens** — covered in Unit 6.

sections.title: Japanese money and how to say it

blocks.text: Japan still relies heavily on cash, and you need to recognize the denominations quickly in your hand. Every amount is said with えん at the end.

blocks.title: Practicing まん quickly
items: The easiest way to read big prices: split the number every **four** digits from the right, not three. 250,000 → 25|0000 → にじゅうごまん.
Roughly, 1,000 yen is somewhere around 6–7 US dollars (depending on the exchange rate). So when you see 一万円, think of a decent restaurant dinner — not pocket change.
Five-minute drill: open a Japanese shopping app and read ten prices aloud. It's the most effective number practice you can do on your own.

blocks.text: Japanese cashiers say the same sentences every day, and they're long and respectful. You don't need to be able to say them — you only need to **recognize** them and know the short answer.

head: What you hear
What it means
Your short answer
rows: [ふくろは|Fukuro wa] [いりますか|irimasu ka]。
[はい|Hai] / [だいじょうぶです|Daijōbu desu]。
[ポイントカードは|Pointo kādo wa]？
Do you have a points card?
[げんきんで|Genkin de]。 / [カードで|Kādo de]。

blocks.title: Three emergency phrases
items: **[だいじょうぶです|Daijōbu desu]。** — “I'm fine / no need.” Politely declines anything.
**[けっこうです|Kekkō desu]。** — “That's all, thanks.” Declines an extra offer.
**[もういちど|Mō ichido] [おねがいします|onegaishimasu]。** — “Once more, please.” The most useful sentence of your first week in Japan.
